text.p: Australia's resources industry is a wealth producer which is being held back by over regulation, according to the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX).

"The (resources) industry suffers the handicap of over regulation which is one of the significant impediments to adding value," Richard Marsh, the ASX's executive director, companies told a mining conference on Friday.

"If significant sovereign risk is added to the inherent risk of mining developments, Australia is surely going to face problems in attracting overseas development capital," Marsh told an Australian Mining '96 conference.
Marsh said the overall complexity of regulation facing companies was now a real problem.

"The issue of risk and regulation and their effects on wealth creation are a concern but there have been developments in Australia recently that have introduced into investors' minds, the question of sovereign risk," Marsh said.
"This particularly affects the mining industry because of its reliance on security of tenure," he said. "Australia is a resource-rich country with problems," Marsh said.
The Australian Stock Exchange recognised the level of risk attached to the resources sector differed from the rest of the market, Marsh said.

"Ensuring that the market has integrity, and is seen to have integrity and confining the risk to the inherent risks of the enterprise, is vital to attracting investors and particularly overseas investors," Marsh said.
Foreign investors accounted for 32.5 percent of share purchases on the Australian market and contributed A$7 billion of new capital to the market in 1995/96, he said.
Resource stocks comprised more than one third of the total capitalisation of the Australian stockmarket- "an extraordinary percentage," Marsh said.
In most other markets, resources accounted for only about 10 percent of capitalisation, he said.
"But the perception seems to be that the mining industry is a wanton destroyer of the environment - not a wealth producer for the country," Marsh said.
Marsh said on present indications, the value of capital raisings in the current year to June 30, 1997 was likely to be higher than in 1995/96.

Raisings this year have included the second half of Commonwealth Bank of Australia, worth more than A$4 billion. He said possible listings included Optus Communications, Ten Network, Colonial Mutual and the possible one-third privatisation of Telstra.
"These, together with National Mutual which listed recently, could constitute a value of around A$12 billion," Marsh said.
Marsh also said the ASX was seeking ways to make it easier for growth small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to seek equity investments on the local stockmarket.
"ASX is currently assessing whether its expertise could be applied to develop a secondary market or other mechanism tailored for growth SMEs," Marsh said.
Options included a matching service for equity seekers and equity investors or establishing an alternative stock market for quoting and trading SME shares, he said.
